In this episode of the Serious Sellers Podcast, Bradley Sutton meets longtime friends and business partners Daniel Gray and Kristian Ball in Chester, England. When rising energy costs squeezed their digital billboard business, they turned to Amazon to generate additional income. Their early success reselling payment terminals helped open the door, but repeated intellectual property issues pushed them toward building their own brands. They report reaching $2 million in turnover during their first year on Amazon. Their private label journey came with expensive lessons. A hair powder product struggled against established competitors, while a slug trap enjoyed strong initial sales before demand weakened in subsequent years. Their sports training brand, Skillbox, grew from a problem they understood firsthand: keeping their children engaged in football practice. By turning training exercises into a dice game, they created a product that sold out within two weeks of its Christmas launch. Their nasal strip product followed a similar approach, addressing Kristian’s frustration with strips that would not stay on during exercise. items.body: Why does this $3.5M Amazon seller spend more on Sponsored Brands than Sponsored Products? Learn the strategy that surprised Bradley, plus approach to European expansion and premium branding. ► Watch The Podcasts On YouTube: https://www.youtube.com/@Helium10?sub_confirmation=1 ► Instagram: instagram.com/serioussellerspodcast ► Free Amazon Seller Chrome Extension: https://h10.me/extension ► Sign Up For Helium 10: https://h10.me/signup (Use SSP10 To Save 10% For Life) ► Learn How To Sell on Amazon: https://h10.me/ft Can you build a multimillion-dollar Amazon business selling something as competitive as smartphone screen protectors? In this episode of the Serious Sellers Podcast, Bradley Sutton meets returning guest Amina Salakhova at Swords Castle in Dublin, Ireland, to explore how she and her husband have done exactly that. With approximately $3.5 million in sales and their sights set on $4 million, Amina shares how expanding across Europe has helped their business thrive. Germany leads their sales, followed by France and Italy, while smaller marketplaces such as Belgium and Ireland offer opportunities to establish a presence early. Her approach to localization goes beyond translation, combining keyword research from Helium 10’s Cerebro and Magnet with ChatGPT to create listings around the terms local shoppers actually use. Competing in a crowded category also means giving customers a reason to choose your product. Amina explains how premium screen protectors, thoughtful packaging, installation kits, and clear instructions help justify higher prices and encourage repeat purchases.
